title: AI agent
summary: AI agents are systems built on AI models that pursue a goal, use tools and act on someone's behalf. What they do depends on the context they are given.
text: AI agents are systems built on AI models that pursue a goal, use tools and act on someone's behalf; for short, the rest of this playbook calls them agents. What is new for knowledge management is this reader: agents now consume a company's knowledge directly, and act on it at scale. What they do depends on the context they are given, and that context has to be steered and mastered, not left to chance (Dynamic context). Around the fundamentals of knowledge management, agents change three things: the reader, the scale and the economics (What agents change). As AI moves from answering to acting, delegating to an agent at scale means accepting that it will act on people's behalf, across many tasks, without every step being checked, while accountability remains human; delegation is therefore gradual (Three levels of delegation).

title: Auditable knowledge construction
summary: Principle 5, extending quality assured by the domain. Knowledge quality is read through traceability: who proposed each change, who validated it, from which sources, and how to revert it.
text: The fifth principle extends the way the Data Mesh treats quality, which it entrusts to the domains, with explicit quality metrics, rather than to the central certification of "golden" datasets. Where data quality is measured by metrics and service levels, knowledge quality is read through traceability: who proposed each change, who validated it, from which sources, and how to revert it. Among the management challenges, auditable construction asks how every contribution is proposed, reviewed, merged and reversed (The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh). See also Traceability. Part of the The five principles.

title: Codification vs personalisation
summary: Hansen, Nohria and Tierney distinguished storing knowledge in documents from connecting the people who hold it. AI loosens that trade-off: the expert stays in charge, the machine does the clerical work.
text: In 1999, Morten Hansen, Nitin Nohria and Thomas Tierney distinguished two strategies: codification, which stores knowledge in documents, and personalisation, which connects the people who hold it. Most companies, they argued, should choose a dominant one. AI changes that last trade-off. When agents can draft, link and maintain pages, codification no longer has to come at the expense of the people who know: the expert stays in charge, the machine does the clerical work. AI loosens another constraint. Organising knowledge has often meant heavy upfront work on classification and ontology before anything could be used. A base no longer has to wait for them: they can be built in parallel, with agents proposing structures and people validating them, so that the structure does not merely mirror the machine's own reading. Work starts on small perimeters (see Start small, and real).

title: Bases that coexist
summary: As bases multiply, the answer is coexistence rather than fusion. Each base keeps its owner, charter and pace; bases share identifiers, metadata and a common way to be reached.
text: Coexistence opens several uses at once: - some agents consume a base for what it contains, to answer a question or carry out a task; - others analyse a base on its own, to measure its coverage, its freshness or its gaps; - others read several bases in a combined context of use, where overlaps and contradictions between domains become visible and can be sent back to the owners concerned. Merging the bases would lose that view; letting them coexist keeps it. See Federated knowledge governance and Organised fragmentation.

title: Compiled knowledge (LLM wiki)
summary: The pages of a base are the compiled layer Andrej Karpathy described as an "LLM wiki": knowledge assembled once and kept up to date, rather than reassembled at every question.
text: In a Knowledge base, pages hold the consolidated knowledge, in an open, readable format, each page linked to its sources. This is the compiled layer Andrej Karpathy described as an "LLM wiki": knowledge assembled once and kept up to date, rather than reassembled at every question. In Karpathy's pattern, as the playbook summarises it, a language model reads raw sources and integrates them into a persistent, interlinked Markdown wiki, noting contradictions and checking for stale claims, while a human curates sources and asks questions. This wiki itself follows that pattern.

title: Context engineering
summary: Since 2025, practitioners have moved from prompt engineering to context engineering, the discipline of choosing what goes into a model's working memory. The Knowledge Mesh adds its organisational side.
text: Getting the best out of a language model was first a matter of prompt engineering: a role, a mission, a few paragraphs of background written by hand into a prompt. Practitioners have since moved on to context engineering, the discipline of choosing what goes into a model's working memory. The shift is right about one thing: the quality of an answer depends on the context more than on the model. The Knowledge Mesh adds the organisational side that context engineering calls for: where good context comes from, and who stands behind it. That organisational side is Dynamic context. The notion is drawn from Anthropic's writing on context engineering.

title: Data, information, knowledge
summary: Data records facts, information gives them meaning in a given context, and knowledge is what lets someone act on them. Knowledge carries judgement, and judgement always belongs to someone.
text: Thomas Davenport and Laurence Prusak described knowledge as "a fluid mix of framed experience, values, contextual information, and expert insight". That is why knowledge cannot be reduced to well-organised data. The classic pyramid, which stacks data, information, knowledge and wisdom as successive refinements, is a useful picture, but it has been rightly criticised for that very shortcut (Ackoff (1989); Frické (2009), the DIKW pyramid and its critique). Knowledge carries judgement, and judgement always belongs to someone, which is where the Knowledge Owner comes in. Data tells an agent what the company records. Knowledge tells it what the company means.

title: Data Mesh
summary: Zhamak Dehghani's answer to the limits of centralised data platforms: four principles, presented as technology-agnostic, held together by shared standards and a common platform.
text: In 2019, Zhamak Dehghani described what many data teams had lived through: a central data lake run by highly specialised engineers, cut off from the business domains that produce and understand the data. The central team became a bottleneck, while the people who knew the data had no ownership of it. Her answer was a paradigm shift, in architecture and organisation alike, not a better lake. In 2020 she formalised four principles: 1. domain-oriented decentralised data ownership and architecture; 2. data as a product; 3. self-serve data infrastructure as a platform; 4. federated computational governance. She presented them as a technology-agnostic model: tools appear as examples, and practices and technologies are expected to vary while the principles remain. The mesh is not a landscape of fragmented silos but an intentionally designed distribution, held together by shared standards for interoperability and a common platform. The Knowledge Mesh borrows this architecture openly and transposes the four principles one by one (see The five principles). Its diagnosis comes from the other foundation, knowledge management research.

title: Authority, not probability
summary: What the owner commits to is narrower than truth: "this is what the company holds to be true, as of this date, and I answer for it." Dated, sourced, open to challenge. No owner, no authority.
text: Review does not guarantee truth, and the playbook says pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The owner's commitment is narrower and more useful: what the company holds to be true, as of a date, with someone answering for it. The statement is dated, sourced and open to challenge; it can be corrected, and the correction is traced. A probable answer, improvised at the moment of the question, offers none of that. This is also what makes delegation possible: people entrust an agent with a task when they can see whose knowledge it acts on (Three levels of delegation). The owner turns a probability into a commitment. That is what an organisation can build on, and what an agent can be held to. No owner, no authority: a base without an owner is just one more document, cleaner perhaps, but just as orphaned.

title: Three levels of delegation
summary: Delegating to agents is a gradual decision, taken domain by domain, as trust grows. Assistance, delegation and autopilot are each reached on evidence.
text: Level Who decides Condition to move on Assistance People read the answer and remain the filter Base validated, sources traced Delegation Agents act; every action is traceable to the knowledge it relied on Evaluation results stable over time; owner arbitrates exceptions Autopilot Sources flow into the base without human review, under continuous quality monitoring Proven quality on the domain; ability to quarantine instantly Trust grows as people understand what agents rely on and see results hold over time (Authority, not probability, Traceability). An agent may always protect on its own, for instance by quarantining a doubtful page. It should never loosen a rule on its own.

title: Distributed knowledge
summary: Knowledge management research reached the Data Mesh diagnosis earlier: knowledge is distributed, created close to practice and kept alive by communities, which is why technology alone did not deliver.
aliases: the firm as a distributed knowledge system
text: The second foundation of the Knowledge Mesh is thirty years of research and practice in knowledge management: - Haridimos Tsoukas described the firm in 1996 as a distributed knowledge system that no one, not even management, can grasp as a whole. - Ikujiro Nonaka showed that knowledge is created close to practice, in the interplay between people, not in a central repository (see Knowledge creation cycle (SECI)). - Etienne Wenger located it in communities of practice. - Richard McDermott explained in 1999 why the first wave of knowledge management tools disappointed: technology could store information, but knowledge depends on the people who use it and the communities that keep it alive. This is the same diagnosis the Data Mesh reached for data, from another direction. It leads to the playbook's stance, Organised fragmentation.

title: The document as output
summary: Building a base turns legacy documents into an asset and audits what the organisation knows. Tomorrow, documents are produced from the base; what is generated never flows back without going through the management plane.
text: An entry point. Every organisation sits on years of legacy documents. Building a base turns that sediment into an asset, and the exercise reveals the gaps, duplicates and contradictions no one could see. Preparing knowledge for an agent is, almost by accident, the first real audit of what the organisation knows. A destination. Today, the base is fed by documents. Tomorrow, documents will increasingly be produced from it: an onboarding guide, a policy summary, a client brief, generated on demand as a view of what the base holds. One safeguard follows: what is generated never flows back into the base without going through the management plane (Principle zero); otherwise the base ends up learning from itself. The document is no longer the source of knowledge; it becomes one of its outputs. Between entry and destination, a single base becomes an enabler for many use cases. That is where the return on investment lies: not in one more chatbot, but in an asset that every use draws on.

title: Domain knowledge ownership
summary: Principle 1, transposing domain-oriented ownership. Knowledge is embodied and partly tacit: the owner answers for it, not just stores it.
text: The first principle transposes the Data Mesh's domain-oriented ownership. What changes for knowledge: it is embodied and partly tacit (Tacit and explicit knowledge), so the owner answers for it, not just stores it. It answers the central bottleneck among the Eight failure modes: a central team carrying the work alone while the people who hold the knowledge are out of the loop. In practice, ownership is held by a Knowledge Owner per base. Part of the The five principles.

title: Dynamic context
summary: Context assembled at the moment of use, from governed knowledge bases, within the rights of the person on whose behalf the agent acts. It is the consumption plane at its most demanding.
text: Four properties distinguish dynamic context from a prompt: - Assembled, not written. The agent selects the bases it needs, guided by their charters, and combines them at the point of use. A cross-functional question draws on several domains without a global model negotiated upfront. - Governed at the source. What enters the context has an owner, a date and a status. A quarantined page simply does not appear. - Rights follow the person. An agent sees what the person it serves is allowed to see, no more. - Traceable. Every element points back to a page, and every page to its sources and its owner (Traceability). It requires standard access: open protocols such as the Model Context Protocol let any agent query any base in the same way. The protocol may change; the principle will remain. This is where principle zero pays off. Dynamic context is the consumption plane at its most demanding. It is only as reliable as the management plane behind it. See Principle zero, Grounding and Context engineering.

title: Eight failure modes
summary: The same patterns recur when AI meets the real corpus. Each has a recognisable symptom, a specific cost for agents, and a principle of the playbook that answers it.
text: Failure mode What it looks like What answers it Retrieval without curation A retrieval layer is plugged into existing documents, and answers are corrected at the output, use case by use case. The same error is fixed ten times and never at the source. Principle zero: separate management from consumption (Principle zero) The central bottleneck A central team, whether knowledge, IT or data, carries the work alone, while the people who hold the knowledge are out of the loop. The base ages faster than it is corrected. Domain ownership (Domain knowledge ownership) The frozen snapshot A base is built once, for a project, then left as it is. Nothing says it has gone stale; agents keep answering from it with the same confidence. The lifecycle, and a contract with a review date (Knowledge lifecycle) The accumulation trap Content keeps growing, generated content included, and nothing is ever retired. Every new page dilutes the ones that matter. Retirement as a step of the lifecycle (Knowledge lifecycle) The tool-first programme A platform is bought in place of an organisation. No one embodies the knowledge, practices do not change, and the tool fills with content no one stands behind. The Knowledge Owner, and the change in roles (Knowledge Owner) The canonical model fantasy A single taxonomy, a single vocabulary, a single model is imposed on every domain. Local meanings are flattened, and agents lose the nuance that made the knowledge useful. Composable bases under shared standards (Federated knowledge governance) The open door Knowledge is exposed without regard to who may see it. Not all knowledge is meant for everyone: an agent that reads everything can show one person what was meant for another, or miss what they need. Rights that follow the person (Dynamic context) The untraceable answer The agent answers or acts without saying which source, which version or whose authority it relied on. No one can validate the answer, correct the source, or explain the action afterwards. Grounded context and traceable actions (Traceability) Each of these is a matter of organisation, which technology makes more visible, and more costly, once agents are involved. Each calls for an organisational answer, beyond prompt engineering or a better model. The way the failure modes are named one by one follows Dehghani's description of the failure modes of centralised data platforms.

title: Federated knowledge governance
summary: Principle 4, transposing federated computational governance. The goal is not to merge bases but to make them composable, through shared identifiers, metadata and open access protocols.
text: The fourth principle transposes federated computational governance. For knowledge, the goal is not to merge bases but to make them composable: shared identifiers, metadata and open access protocols. It answers the canonical model fantasy among the Eight failure modes, where a single taxonomy is imposed on every domain. It relies on a governance that embraces several interpretive contexts rather than one canonical model. In practice, bases coexist rather than merge (Bases that coexist) and stay portable across tools (Interoperability and portability). Part of the The five principles.

title: The five principles
summary: The first four principles transpose those of the Data Mesh. The fifth extends the way the Data Mesh entrusts quality to the domains, rather than to central certification of golden datasets.
text: Data Mesh principle Knowledge Mesh principle What changes for knowledge Domain-oriented ownership Domain knowledge ownership Knowledge is embodied and partly tacit: the owner answers for it, not just stores it Data as a product Knowledge as a self-describing product Two kinds of consumers, people and agents; no base without a charter Self-serve data platform Self-serve knowledge platform AI is not only hosted on the platform, it works inside it: drafts, links, flags contradictions Federated computational governance Federated knowledge governance The goal is not to merge bases but to make them composable: shared identifiers, metadata, open access protocols Data product quality, assured by the domain Auditable knowledge construction Knowledge quality is read through traceability: who proposed each change, who validated it, from which sources, and how to revert it The principles say what a Knowledge Mesh is; the The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh say what it must make possible.

title: Fundamentals before solutions
summary: Solutions already address many challenges. The playbook starts one step earlier, with what must be true of knowledge for people and agents to rely on it; the answer shapes the choice of tools, and outlasts it.
text: Enterprise search, verified knowledge bases, content platforms with built-in agents and semantic layers already address many of the The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh; many are useful, some very good. The playbook deliberately starts one step earlier, with the fundamentals that let an organisation choose, combine and replace them. In an agentic and hybrid world, where people and agents work from the same knowledge, one question comes first: what must be true of knowledge for both to rely on it? The answer shapes the choice of tools, and outlasts it.

title: Grounding
summary: Grounding is the shared basis on which joint action rests. Decisions and actions must be anchored in knowledge the company holds to be true, not in what a model finds plausible.
text: Before an agent can decide or act, it needs to stand on solid ground: facts, rules and reasons that are established, dated and owned. Linguists Herbert Clark and Susan Brennan called the process of building that shared basis grounding: the mutual knowledge on which any joint action rests. The same word is now used in AI for anchoring an answer in sources. The overlap is not a coincidence: whether between two people or between a company and its agents, nobody can act together without first agreeing on what is taken to be true. Grounding separates an answer that sounds right from a decision that can be defended. It requires knowledge that someone stands behind (the management plane, see Authority, not probability) and a way to bring it to the agent at the moment it acts (Dynamic context). No delegation without grounding. Decisions and actions must be anchored in knowledge the company holds to be true, not in what a model finds plausible.

title: Knowledge as a pillar of AI
summary: To understand a situation, an agent needs data, what the company records, and knowledge, what it means and how to act on it. Knowledge deserves the same status as data.
text: The playbook's thesis fits in one line: Knowledge is a pillar of AI at scale, alongside data. It must be managed as infrastructure, separately from the way it is consumed. The HP quote named, in the 1990s, a gap every large organisation recognises: a company knows far more than it manages to use. Expertise stays in one corner, know-how does not travel, people spend their time searching. The ambition it expressed has not changed: bring the right knowledge, in the right shape and quality, to the right place at the right time. What has changed is who needs it. A colleague can ask a colleague; an agent cannot. What a company knows but has not made accessible, an agent will never know, and an agent that is not grounded in that knowledge can only produce what is plausible, not what is reliable (see Grounding). The first stake is therefore context. An agent needs two things: data, what the company records, and knowledge, what it means and how to act on it (see Data, information, knowledge). Every company that has tried to put AI to work has learned the lesson about data, "garbage in, garbage out", even if it is not quite that simple: data quality, ownership and governance are now standard items of any AI programme. Knowledge, here meaning what lets someone act well (the rule, the exception, the reason behind both, last year's trade-off and why), received less attention: the discipline exists, but it had no seat at the table (see Why knowledge was underestimated). AI also changes the volume. More content does not mean more knowledge: the more content there is, the more it needs to be traced, qualified and sorted. Knowledge management itself is mature, up to an international standard (ISO 30401). What it long lacked were tools people truly adopt. AI changes that: before it helps consume knowledge, it can help manage it.

title: Knowledge as a self-describing product
summary: Principle 2, transposing data as a product. There are two kinds of consumers, people and agents, and no base without a charter.
text: The second principle transposes data as a product. A knowledge base serves two kinds of consumers, people and agents, and none exists without a charter. The charter states the base's purpose, owner, audience and how it is built. It commits the owner, guides the agent that drafts the pages and tells other agents when to consult the base (see Knowledge base). The idea draws on Dehghani's data products that are discoverable, trustworthy and self-describing, with service level objectives, which also underpin the contract of a base. Part of the The five principles.

title: Knowledge base
summary: The unit and asset of the mesh: small enough to have one owner and one purpose, complete enough to be useful on its own. It has seven parts.
text: A knowledge base has seven parts: - A domain and a purpose : what it covers, for whom, and what it deliberately does not cover. - A charter : purpose, owner, audience, how it is built. It commits the owner, guides the agent that drafts the pages and tells other agents when to consult the base. - A Knowledge Owner : the person who answers for it (Knowledge Owner). - Sources : the documents, sites and contributions it is built from, each inventoried. - Pages : the consolidated knowledge, in an open, readable format, each page linked to its sources (Compiled knowledge (LLM wiki)). - A contract : review frequency, how fast a source change reaches the pages, the minimum quality guaranteed. Its health is measured against that contract. - States : active, under review, quarantined, retired. A page or a whole base can be withdrawn from use without stopping everything else. A base is both an entry point and a destination (The document as output), and bases live together by coexistence rather than fusion (Bases that coexist). See Figure 5: The seven parts of a knowledge base.

title: Knowledge lifecycle
summary: Knowledge is born, lives and dies. Six stages mark that life, capture, consolidate, validate, serve, review and retire, each with someone responsible; retirement is the one most often forgotten.
text: Managing knowledge means following it through its whole life, from the moment it enters a base to the moment it is withdrawn. 1. Capture : bring in sources, legacy documents, interviews, decisions. 2. Consolidate : deduplicate, link, structure into pages. 3. Validate : the Knowledge Owner commits to what the page says. 4. Serve : expose it to people and agents, according to rights. 5. Review : refresh on a known cadence or when a source changes. 6. Retire : withdraw what is obsolete, and say so. The last stage is the one most often forgotten. An outdated document left in an index silently becomes a wrong answer. Living knowledge must be allowed to die. The lifecycle answers two Eight failure modes, the frozen snapshot and the accumulation trap. A Knowledge base expresses it through its contract and its states (active, under review, quarantined, retired). See Figure 3: The lifecycle.

title: Knowledge Mesh
summary: A decentralised network of living knowledge bases, owned by business domains, each described by a charter and built through auditable contributions from people and agents, federated by common standards.
text: A Knowledge Mesh is a decentralised network of living knowledge bases, owned by business domains, each described by a charter and built through auditable contributions from people and agents, federated by common standards so that everyone, human or agent, shares the same governed context. It stands on two foundations: the architecture of the Data Mesh and the diagnosis of knowledge management research. It rests on The five principles and must address a set of The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh. Two vocabulary choices avoid confusion. The Knowledge Mesh is the whole: the network, the platform and the common rules. The Knowledge base is the unit: what a domain builds, owns and serves. One does not exist without the other. No company starts with a mesh: it is a The mesh is a trajectory. See Figure 4: From raw sources to use cases.

title: Knowledge Owner
summary: The person accountable for a base, and the central idea of the playbook: knowledge needs a face. Agents take on most of the stewardship; the owner keeps what cannot be delegated.
text: A language model produces the most plausible answer; a company needs an answer someone stands behind. Knowledge needs a face. Embodiment is what makes governance real: a base can be governed because someone decides for it, and audited because someone answers for it. Without that person, rules apply to no one and an audit finds no one to question. The Knowledge Owner embodies the base: its scope, its choices and its limits. Data management separates the owner, accountable for an asset, from the steward, who looks after it day to day. In a Knowledge Mesh, agents take on most of the stewardship: they draft pages, check sources, flag contradictions and assess freshness. The owner keeps what cannot be delegated: Responsibility What it means Orient Decide what the base is for, what it covers and what it does not Arbitrate Settle contradictions and ambiguous cases, which agents escalate with a diagnosis Commit Validate what the base says, and put their name on it Listen Receive what consumers report, agents and people alike: drift, gaps, errors, unanswered questions Retire Decide what is no longer valid The owner does not reread everything: clear-cut changes go through, the owner handles the exceptions. Agents that consume a base are its most attentive readers; their signals flow back to the owner. One condition is not negotiable: the time an owner spends on a base must be recognised as part of their job. Otherwise the role becomes a chore, and the base slowly dies. See Authority, not probability and Figure 6: Agents and the Knowledge Owner.

title: The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh
summary: The principles say what a Knowledge Mesh is; the challenges say what it must make possible. Fourteen questions fall into three families: managing knowledge, consuming it, and federating the bases.
text: The challenges are stated as questions, because each organisation will answer them in its own way. Managing knowledge. The first family concerns the management plane (Principle zero): how knowledge enters a base, how someone commits to it, and how it stays true over time. Challenge What it asks Compiling the legacy How do scattered documents become sourced, consolidated pages? Committing Who validates, and how is that commitment visible to people and machines? Keeping it alive How are contradictions, staleness and gaps detected, and by whom? Lifecycle How is knowledge reviewed, quarantined and retired? Auditable construction How is every contribution proposed, reviewed, merged and reversed? Consuming knowledge. The second family concerns the consumption plane: how people and agents draw on knowledge at the moment they need it, within the right limits, and with a trace of what they relied on. Challenge What it asks Assembling context How does an agent select and combine the right bases at the moment of use? Rights How do access rights follow the person an agent acts for? Traceability How can any answer or action be traced to the knowledge it relied on? Reaching the tacit How are the people who hold what is not written found and connected? Federating the mesh. The third family concerns the mesh itself: how bases owned by different domains are found, live side by side, and keep their value as tools change. Challenge What it asks Discovery How are bases, their charters and their owners found? Coexistence How can bases be consumed alone or in combination, and analysed side by side, without being merged? Shared standards Which identifiers, metadata and protocols let bases compose? Quality How is the health of a base measured against its contract and its evaluation set? Portability How does knowledge outlive the tools that built it?

title: The mesh is a trajectory
summary: No company starts with a mesh: it starts with a common foundation, and the mesh appears as domains take ownership one after another. Centralise the means, decentralise the knowledge.
text: A mesh usually starts with a common foundation: one platform, a few standards, the first bases, often run by a small central team. That is consistent with the mesh: Dehghani herself treats the self-serve platform as a precondition of it (Self-serve knowledge platform). Much of that platform can be assembled from existing tools; what has to be built is the way they are composed, and the standards that let bases move between them. The mesh appears as domains take ownership one after another, and as the central team moves from building bases to providing the platform and the rules. Starting centrally is a sound first step; the aim is to move beyond it. Centralise the means, decentralise the knowledge.

title: What the Knowledge Mesh values
summary: Five preferences sum up the playbook's answer. Each favours a way of working without dismissing the alternative: the mesh simply puts the first column first.
aliases: five things the Knowledge Mesh values
text: The Knowledge Mesh values… …more than Because Curating the source Correcting the answer A correction made once, upstream, serves every use downstream Committed knowledge Plausible answers An agent can rely on what someone stands behind; from the rest, it can only guess Owned bases A single repository Knowledge stays close to those who hold it, and bases coexist rather than merge Retiring knowledge Accumulating content What is withdrawn on time protects every answer that follows Traceable action Opaque assistance What can be traced can be understood, corrected and trusted The second column still has value: answers will always need some correction, and a shared repository can be useful. Each line echoes the Eight failure modes and the separation of Principle zero.

title: What stays open
summary: The playbook is meant to be extended by those who put it to work. Four questions remain open, about measuring value, the owner role, simplicity and a single entry point.
text: - How can the value of a living knowledge base be measured by its use, rather than by the volume of pages it holds? - How can the Knowledge Owner role become a form of recognition rather than one more duty, and how far can stewardship be handed to agents while keeping the human judgement that makes a base worth trusting? - How can the approach stay simple, and rely on open standards rather than build its own? - On the consumption side, how can fragmented knowledge be consumed through a simple, single entry point, without recentralising how it is managed? The aim is a shared vision more than a single recipe: the smallest set of principles from which each organisation can build its own Knowledge Mesh, with its own tools and at its own pace. The playbook closes on Montaigne's well-made mind: knowledge that is sorted, organised, owned and kept alive, so that it can be used with judgement.

title: Organised fragmentation
summary: The playbook's stance: accept fragmentation and organise it, rather than pursue the single base. Knowledge is fragmented because it is distributed, situated and alive.
text: Accept fragmentation and organise it, rather than pursue the single base. Knowledge is fragmented because it is distributed, situated and alive. Centralising it fights its nature; organising the fragments works with it. The stance follows from Distributed knowledge and from the Data Mesh, which is an intentionally designed distribution rather than a set of silos. Work starts on small perimeters; fragments are brought together at the moment of use (see Dynamic context) and enriched in the meantime. Bases coexist rather than merge (Bases that coexist), and the playbook values owned bases more than a single repository (What the Knowledge Mesh values).

title: Interoperability and portability
summary: A knowledge base is built to last longer than the technologies that serve it. The test: if the tool that built a base disappeared tomorrow, could the knowledge be read, moved and served by another one?
text: Models, agent frameworks and access protocols will change several times over the life of a base, and knowledge must be able to follow without starting over. That calls for simple, open and evolvable formats: readable text pages, explicit metadata, stable identifiers, links that make sense to a person as well as to a machine, and access through open protocols rather than proprietary connectors. If the answer is no, the company does not own its knowledge; its tool does. Interoperability governed by global standards is a foundational pillar of distributed systems in Dehghani's description of the data mesh. See Federated knowledge governance.

title: Principle zero
summary: Managing knowledge and consuming it are two different jobs, in two planes with different roles and rhythms. The separation concerns roles and rhythms, not teams.
text: The playbook uses the image of an encyclopedia: editors choose entries, check sources, settle disputes and retire what is wrong; readers come with their own questions and never see the editorial process. In daily practice, companies rarely worked this way. To find something, one had to understand the logic of whoever filed it, and every filing scheme was a bet on how people would search. Research at Bellcore showed how fragile that bet is: two people rarely choose the same word for the same thing (Furnas et al. (1987), The Vocabulary Problem). AI breaks that link: people can ask in their own words against a corpus organised once, consistently. Management plane Consumption plane Purpose Build, validate, keep alive, retire Answer, assist, act, produce Who Knowledge Owners, helped by agents Employees, assistants, business agents, document generators Pace Deliberate: reviewed, versioned, dated Instant: at the moment of the question Key question What do we hold to be true, and who answers for it? What does this person or agent need, right now? Measured by Coverage, freshness, contradictions resolved Usefulness, adoption, time saved Three consequences make the approach pragmatic: - Each plane can change without breaking the other. Models, chat tools and agent frameworks will change many times; a well-managed knowledge base survives them all. Conversely, a new use case does not require reorganising the knowledge. - One effort, many uses. Knowledge kept once serves a newcomer, a support agent and a generated report alike. The investment is made in the management plane and pays off in every consumption. - A clear boundary. Consumers read; they do not rewrite while they work. What they run into, a gap or a contradiction, goes back to the management plane as a ticket. The base learns from its use without feeding on its own answers. The Data Mesh offers a precedent: it keeps operational and analytical data in two planes, integrated yet separate, because they serve different needs; and Dehghani is clear that this technical separation should not separate the organisation: the same domains look after both. The separation proposed here works the same way. RAG, chat interfaces and agents all belong to the consumption plane; they need something upstream to read. The same holds for the ways of bringing knowledge to a model (training, retrieval, web search, fine-tuning or distillation): each has its value, its cost and its prerequisites, and knowledge built into a model's weights is also tied to that model and hard to trace back to a source. Whatever the mode, what an agent can rely on depends on the quality and traceability of what it draws from: a matter of construction before consumption. See Figure 1: Principle zero.

title: Knowledge creation cycle (SECI)
summary: Knowledge is created as it moves between tacit and explicit forms: socialisation, externalisation, combination, internalisation. AI excels at combination and helps externalisation; socialisation remains a human affair.
text: Nonaka and Takeuchi showed that knowledge is created as it moves between its tacit and explicit forms: - Socialisation : people share know-how by working together. - Externalisation : they put it into words. - Combination : explicit pieces are assembled into larger wholes. - Internalisation : people make explicit knowledge their own by using it. Read with agents in mind, the cycle is uneven. AI excels at combination and is a strong ally for externalisation: an interview, a meeting or a recorded walkthrough can become a draft page. Socialisation remains a human affair: people still learn from people. A knowledge strategy that overlooks this produces clean pages and empty expertise.

title: Self-serve knowledge platform
summary: Principle 3, transposing the self-serve data platform. AI is not only hosted on the platform, it works inside it: it drafts, links and flags contradictions.
text: The third principle transposes the self-serve data platform. For knowledge, AI is not only hosted on the platform; it works inside it, drafting pages, linking sources and flagging contradictions. Dehghani treats the self-serve platform as a precondition of the mesh. Much of it can be assembled from existing tools; what has to be built is the way they are composed, and the standards that let bases move between them (see The mesh is a trajectory and Interoperability and portability). Part of the The five principles.

title: Start small, and real
summary: The first steps aim at a first base that is useful quickly, owned by someone and measured from the start: one domain, one owner, a one-page charter, the legacy compiled, an evaluation set.
text: 1. Pick one domain with a real pain: questions asked again and again, answers that vary from one person to the next. 2. Name one Knowledge Owner who wants the role, and give them time for it (Knowledge Owner). 3. Write the charter in one page: purpose, audience, scope, what is out of scope. 4. Compile the legacy : let agents turn existing documents into a first set of sourced pages, then let the owner validate them. Expect to discover gaps; that is part of the value. 5. Build an evaluation set : the questions the domain actually receives, with the answers the owner expects. Every change, of content or of model, is then measured against it. What is learned on one domain can serve the next (The mesh is a trajectory).

title: Tacit and explicit knowledge
summary: Part of what experts know will never be fully written down. A Knowledge Mesh aims to make explicit what can be, and to show clearly where the rest lives: with whom, in which community.
text: "We can know more than we can tell," wrote Michael Polanyi. Part of what experts know will never be fully written down. A Knowledge Mesh aims to make explicit what can be, and to show clearly where the rest lives: with whom, in which community. This matters more with agents, because the main new consumer is a machine that knows only what has been made explicit (What agents change). Reaching the tacit, finding and connecting the people who hold what is not written, is one of the consumption challenges of the mesh (The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh). See Figure 2: What can be written, and where the rest lives.

title: Traceability
summary: Every element of an agent's context points back to a page, and every page to its sources and its owner, so that whatever an agent relied on can be inspected afterwards.
text: Traceability runs through the playbook: the untraceable answer is one of the Eight failure modes; auditable construction is the fifth principle (Auditable knowledge construction); traceable is one of the four properties of Dynamic context; and traceable action is one of the things the mesh values (What the Knowledge Mesh values). Regulation points the same way, within a narrower scope. For high-risk AI systems, the EU AI Act requires automatic logging to ensure the traceability of how a system functions, effective human oversight, and the retention of logs by deployers. Most knowledge agents will not fall into that category. It is still reasonable to aim for the same capability everywhere: being able to trace what an agent did, and which knowledge it relied on, is what makes it possible to understand, validate and trust the adoption of agents at scale. At the delegation level, every action is traceable to the knowledge it relied on (Three levels of delegation).

title: Why knowledge was underestimated
summary: Four reasons, offered as a practitioner's reading rather than a measured finding: the model seemed to know, retrieval was treated as engineering, governance followed data, and knowledge management was out of the room.
aliases: why it was underestimated in the move to AI
text: The playbook gives four reasons, and states that they are a practitioner's reading, not a measured finding. - The model seemed to know. Large language models answer fluently on almost any subject, yet know nothing specific about a company until it is given to them. - Retrieval was treated as engineering. RAG framed the problem as search (chunking, indexing, ranking). Authority, freshness and contradiction were left to sources that often nobody owned. - Governance followed data. AI programmes inherited the data governance agenda (privacy, quality, lineage, bias) and often stopped there. Unstructured knowledge sat between data teams, IT and the business. - Knowledge management was out of the room. It had often become a support function, rarely part of AI steering. The cost shows up at scale. A widely discussed MIT report finds that most organisations see no measurable return from generative AI, and points to systems that do not retain context or learn from feedback. Pilots run on clean, curated material; at scale, agents meet the real corpus, where the Eight failure modes appear.

title: What agents change
summary: The fundamentals of knowledge management stay. Agents change three things around them, the reader, the scale and the economics, and the effort moves to validation.
aliases: what genuinely changes with AI agents
text: Agents change three things around the fundamentals of knowledge management: - The reader. The main new consumer is a machine that knows only what has been made explicit (see Tacit and explicit knowledge). - The scale. An error no longer misleads one colleague; it travels through every process an agent touches. - The economics. Drafting and maintaining pages becomes cheap, so the effort moves to validation. What stays What changes with agents Knowledge is partly tacit and lives in people and communities The main new consumer is a machine that knows only what has been made explicit Knowledge needs owners, a lifecycle and retirement Authority, date and status must be readable by machines, not only by colleagues Codification has a cost AI collapses the cost of drafting, linking and maintaining pages; the bottleneck moves to validation Errors in documentation mislead some readers Errors propagate systematically, to every agent, in every process People find their way around gaps Agents do not call a colleague: gaps become wrong answers or wrong actions Agents raise the bar upstream. The effort moves from consuming knowledge to building it: owned, validated, dated and traceable before any agent reads it.

title: Andrej Karpathy
summary: Described the "LLM wiki" pattern, the compiled layer behind the pages of a knowledge base, and the pattern this wiki follows.
text: Karpathy's "LLM wiki" is the compiled layer behind the pages of a Knowledge base: knowledge assembled once and kept up to date, rather than reassembled at every question (Compiled knowledge (LLM wiki)). This wiki applies the same pattern to the playbook itself: a raw source kept intact, compiled pages, a schema, an index and a log.

title: Anthropic
summary: Cited for two things: the notion of context engineering, which dynamic context extends, and the Model Context Protocol, as an example of open access standard.
text: The playbook draws on two Anthropic publications: one on Context engineering, which Dynamic context extends with its organisational side, and the announcement of the Model Context Protocol, cited as an example of an open access standard.

title: EU AI Act
summary: Requires automatic logging, human oversight and log retention for high-risk AI systems; the playbook extends these as good practice for all agents.
text: Articles 12, 14 and 26 require high-risk AI systems to log events automatically, to be designed for effective human oversight, and their deployers to keep the logs. Most knowledge agents will not fall into the high-risk category; the playbook still finds it reasonable to aim for the same capability everywhere (Traceability).

title: Ikujiro Nonaka
summary: Theorist of organisational knowledge creation who, with Hirotaka Takeuchi, described the SECI cycle; the playbook takes from him the insight that knowledge is created between people.
text: Nonaka showed that knowledge is created close to practice, in the interplay between people, not in a central repository (Distributed knowledge). With Takeuchi, he described knowledge creation as a conversion between tacit and explicit forms: socialisation, externalisation, combination and internalisation (Knowledge creation cycle (SECI)). The playbook rereads that cycle with agents in mind.

title: ISO 30401
summary: The international standard for knowledge management systems, cited to show that knowledge management is an established, standardised discipline.
text: The standard sets requirements for establishing, maintaining and improving a knowledge management system, treating it as a managed system with leadership, roles and continual improvement. The playbook cites it as evidence that the discipline is mature (Knowledge as a pillar of AI): the methods exist.

title: Lew Platt
summary: Chief executive of Hewlett-Packard in the 1990s, to whom the sentence "If only HP knew what HP knows" is attributed; it frames the gap and the ambition of the playbook.
aliases: If only HP knew what HP knows
text: "If only HP knew what HP knows, we would be three times more productive." The sentence named a gap every large organisation recognises: a company knows far more than it manages to use. The playbook notes that the quotation is attributed, reported in several variants, with no primary source located. Platt was talking about people, who could still ask a colleague; agents cannot (Knowledge as a pillar of AI).

title: Michael Polanyi
summary: Introduced tacit knowledge with the observation that "we can know more than we can tell".
text: Polanyi's observation grounds the playbook's treatment of Tacit and explicit knowledge knowledge: part of what experts know will never be fully written down, so a Knowledge Mesh makes explicit what can be and shows where the rest lives.

title: Michel de Montaigne
summary: "A well-made mind rather than a well-filled one": the playbook closes on Montaigne's ranking of discernment above accumulation.
text: « Plutôt la tête bien faite que bien pleine. » For Montaigne, a well-made mind is the one that can judge, sort and order what it knows, and put it to use. He does not dismiss knowledge; he places discernment above accumulation. The playbook applies this to companies, which have spent decades filling their heads with drives, intranets and document libraries, and which agents now ask for a well-made one (What the Knowledge Mesh values, What stays open).

title: Model Context Protocol
summary: An open protocol introduced in 2024, cited as an example of standard access: it lets any agent query any base in the same way. The protocol may change; the principle will remain.
text: Dynamic context requires standard access to knowledge bases. Open protocols such as the Model Context Protocol let any agent query any base in the same way, rather than through proprietary connectors (Interoperability and portability). In Figure 4: From raw sources to use cases, MCP is the common access layer that serves people and agents by use case.

title: Zhamak Dehghani
summary: Author of the Data Mesh (2019, 2020), whose architecture the Knowledge Mesh openly transposes.
text: In 2019, Zhamak Dehghani described the limits of central data platforms; in 2020 she formalised the four principles of the Data Mesh. Her two texts are cited in seven of the playbook's "Sources & inspirations" boxes. The playbook takes from them: - the failure modes of centralised platforms, named one by one (Eight failure modes); - operational and analytical data as two planes, a precedent for Principle zero; - the four principles, transposed one by one (The five principles), and quality assured by the domains, basis of Auditable knowledge construction; - the data product owner, responsible for the lifecycle of the domain's data (Knowledge Owner); - discoverable, self-describing data products with service level objectives, behind the charter and contract of a Knowledge base; - the self-serve platform as a precondition, basis of the The mesh is a trajectory, and interoperability governed by global standards (Interoperability and portability).

title: Figure 1: Principle zero
summary: Two planes side by side, managing and consuming, linked by an access arrow; what consumers run into, gaps or errors, goes back to the managing plane.
text: What the figure shows. Two boxes side by side. - Managing (left, in the accent colour): a book standing for the knowledge base, a person and an agent. Below: "build · validate · keep alive · retire", and "deliberate, dated". A small legend marks the book as "markdown format". - Consuming (right): a person and an agent, each with a question mark. Below: "answer · assist · act", "people and agents", "instant". - An arrow labelled "MCP / API" goes from managing to consuming. - A dashed arrow returns from consuming to managing, carrying two tags: "gaps" and "errors". What it means. One effort in the management plane serves every use in the consumption plane, and the base learns from its use through feedback rather than from its own answers. See Principle zero.

title: Figure 2: What can be written, and where the rest lives
summary: An iceberg: the written, documented part above the waterline is what the agent sees; the tacit part held by people, below, is most of what the company knows.
text: What the figure shows. An iceberg cut by the waterline. - Above the water, labelled "written, documented": two peaks holding documents. A bracket marks them as "what the agent sees". Some of the documents look faded. - Below the water, labelled "tacit, held by people": a much larger mass containing three people, a speech bubble, a light bulb, a clock and a few documents. - A bracket spanning the whole iceberg reads "what the company knows". What it means. An agent only sees what has been made explicit; most of what the company knows is held by people. A Knowledge Mesh makes explicit what can be, and shows where the rest lives. See Tacit and explicit knowledge.

title: Figure 3: The lifecycle
summary: Six numbered stages from capture to retire, each tagged with who acts, agents, the owner or both; review loops back to capture.
text: What the figure shows. A vertical sequence of six numbered stages, each with its actors and a short line: 1. Capture (agents): agents compile the legacy; people bring interviews. 2. Consolidate (agents): deduplicate, link, structure. 3. Validate (agents, owner): agents check, the owner commits. 4. Serve : to people and agents, according to rights. 5. Review (agents, owner): agents assess freshness, the owner refreshes. 6. Retire (agents, owner, highlighted): agents flag, the owner decides, and says so. A dashed arrow loops from Review back to Capture. What it means. The work is shared: agents carry the volume, the owner commits and decides. Retirement is highlighted because it is the stage most often forgotten. See Knowledge lifecycle.

title: Figure 4: From raw sources to use cases
summary: Layers from bottom to top: traced raw sources, converted to markdown, compiled into domain wikis with an owner each, served through a common MCP access layer to people and agents.
text: What the figure shows. Five layers, read from bottom to top. - Raw sources, traced : documents, a conversation, an email. - Converted to markdown : .md files. - Knowledge bases, a wiki, an owner : two example bases, "HR" and "Legal", each with its owner icon and a wiki of pages, plus a dashed box for "other bases". Dotted lines trace individual pages back to the raw source they come from. - Access : a common band labelled "MCP · access by use cases". - People and agents : a group of people and a cluster of agents, served from the access layer. What it means. Each base is owned by a domain and compiles its own traced sources into a wiki; bases coexist under a common access layer rather than being merged. See Knowledge Mesh, Compiled knowledge (LLM wiki) and Model Context Protocol.

title: Figure 5: The seven parts of a knowledge base
summary: A book at the centre, labelled knowledge base, surrounded by its seven parts: Knowledge Owner, sources, pages, charter, contract, domain and states.
text: What the figure shows. A book in the centre, labelled "knowledge base", with seven labels around it: - Knowledge Owner (top, highlighted): answers for it. - Sources : inventoried. - Pages : linked to sources. - Charter : purpose, audience. - Contract : review, freshness. - Domain : what it covers. - States : active … retired. What it means. A base is more than a set of pages: it has a scope, a charter, an owner, inventoried sources, a contract it is measured against, and states that let any part be withdrawn. See Knowledge base.

title: Figure 6: Agents and the Knowledge Owner
summary: Agents draft from documents, interviews and decisions under the charter; clear-cut changes go straight to the wiki, doubtful ones go to the Knowledge Owner, who arbitrates and commits.
text: What the figure shows. A flow from left to right. - Inputs: documents, interviews, decisions. - An agent ("agents draft") turns them into drafts, framed by a Charter box (purpose, audience). - A decision diamond asks "clear-cut?". - Yes : the change goes straight into the Wiki . - Doubt : the change goes to the Knowledge Owner , drawn as a person holding a validated document, labelled "arbitrates, commits", who then sends it to the Wiki. What it means. The owner does not reread everything: clear-cut changes go through, and the owner handles the exceptions, which keeps the role sustainable. See Knowledge Owner.

title: The Knowledge Mesh Playbook
summary: Knowledge is a pillar of AI at scale, alongside data. It must be managed as infrastructure, separately from the way it is consumed.
text: If only the company knew what it knows. A playbook to bring the right knowledge, in the right shape, to the right place at the right time, for people and AI agents alike. Knowledge management has thirty years of research, an international standard, dedicated roles and a market of tools. What is new is the reader: AI agents now consume a company's knowledge directly, and act on it at scale. What they do depends on the context they are given, and that context has to be steered and mastered, not left to chance. AI agents are systems built on AI models that pursue a goal, use tools and act on someone's behalf (AI agent). Yet organisations preparing for AI invest in data, models and platforms, and often treat knowledge as a side issue (Knowledge as a pillar of AI). The playbook builds a bridge between what knowledge management already knows and what agentic AI now requires. Its organising principle is a separation, Principle zero: managing knowledge is one job, consuming it is another. Its operating model is the Knowledge Mesh, openly inspired by the Data Mesh: knowledge bases owned by domains, each with a charter and a Knowledge Owner who commits to what it says, federated by a few shared standards. Key concepts at a glance Concept Definition in the playbook Management and consumption Two planes: knowledge is built, owned and governed in one, used by people and agents in the other Knowledge base The unit of the mesh: a domain, a charter, an owner, sources, pages, a contract and states Knowledge Owner The person who answers for a base: orients, arbitrates, commits and retires Dynamic context Context assembled at the moment of use, from governed bases, within the user's rights, and traceable; the organisational side of context engineering Knowledge Mesh A network of domain-owned knowledge bases, federated by shared standards What it builds on, and what it adds It builds on It adds Thirty years of knowledge management research, methods and tools, which remain valid That knowledge has been underestimated as a success factor in deploying AI at scale The tacit, human side of knowledge, which lives with people and communities That agents change who consumes knowledge, and therefore what "well managed" must mean The Data Mesh, whose architecture it openly transposes An operating model for knowledge that fits agents, and that each organisation can adapt Today's solutions, which already address many of the challenges described here The fundamentals that let an organisation choose, combine and replace them, in a world where people and agents share the same knowledge How to read it Sections 1 to 4 set the foundations: 1. The underestimated pillar, 2. Principle zero, 3. Where the Knowledge Mesh comes from, 4. Fundamentals we build on. Sections 5 to 8 describe the model, its challenges and its roles: 5. The Knowledge Mesh in brief, 6. The knowledge base, 7. The Knowledge Owner, 8. Dynamic context. Section 9 is the field guide to start: 9. Field guide. The closing section sums up what the Knowledge Mesh values: What it values, what stays open. The foreword explains why the playbook exists: Why this playbook. The playbook borrows the rigour of an academic paper, sources and definitions, in plain language. It is written in its own words: sources mark the landmarks and inspirations behind each part, and the few direct quotations appear in quotation marks. Each part closes with a short box naming the sources it draws on and what it takes from them; the full references are in the catalog under Sources.

title: 3. Where the Knowledge Mesh comes from
summary: Two foundations: the architecture of the Data Mesh and the diagnosis of thirty years of knowledge management research.
text: Structure - The Data Mesh started from the limits of centralisation - Knowledge management research had reached the same diagnosis earlier Key ideas The stance. Accept fragmentation and organise it, rather than pursue the single base. Knowledge is fragmented because it is distributed, situated and alive. Centralising it fights its nature; organising the fragments works with it. Concepts - Data Mesh: Zhamak Dehghani's answer to the limits of centralised data platforms: four principles, presented as technology-agnostic, held together by shared standards and a common platform. - Distributed knowledge: Knowledge management research reached the Data Mesh diagnosis earlier: knowledge is distributed, created close to practice and kept alive by communities, which is why technology alone did not deliver. - Codification vs personalisation: Hansen, Nohria and Tierney distinguished storing knowledge in documents from connecting the people who hold it. AI loosens that trade-off: the expert stays in charge, the machine does the clerical work. - Organised fragmentation: The playbook's stance: accept fragmentation and organise it, rather than pursue the single base. Knowledge is fragmented because it is distributed, situated and alive. title: 4. Fundamentals we build on
summary: Four established ideas become directly operational once agents are the readers: data, information and knowledge; tacit and explicit; the creation cycle; the lifecycle.
text: Structure - Data, information, knowledge - Tacit and explicit - The knowledge creation cycle - The lifecycle Key ideas Key idea. Data tells an agent what the company records. Knowledge tells it what the company means. Concepts - Data, information, knowledge: Data records facts, information gives them meaning in a given context, and knowledge is what lets someone act on them. Knowledge carries judgement, and judgement always belongs to someone. - Tacit and explicit knowledge: Part of what experts know will never be fully written down. A Knowledge Mesh aims to make explicit what can be, and to show clearly where the rest lives: with whom, in which community. - Knowledge creation cycle (SECI): Knowledge is created as it moves between tacit and explicit forms: socialisation, externalisation, combination, internalisation. AI excels at combination and helps externalisation; socialisation remains a human affair. - Knowledge lifecycle: Knowledge is born, lives and dies. Six stages mark that life, capture, consolidate, validate, serve, review and retire, each with someone responsible; retirement is the one most often forgotten. title: 5. The Knowledge Mesh in brief
summary: The definition, five principles transposed from the Data Mesh, and the challenges a Knowledge Mesh must address, in three families.
text: Structure - The challenges a Knowledge Mesh must address - Fundamentals before solutions Key ideas Definition. A Knowledge Mesh is a decentralised network of living knowledge bases, owned by business domains, each described by a charter and built through auditable contributions from people and agents, federated by common standards so that everyone, human or agent, shares the same governed context. Concepts - Knowledge Mesh: A decentralised network of living knowledge bases, owned by business domains, each described by a charter and built through auditable contributions from people and agents, federated by common standards. - The five principles: The first four principles transpose those of the Data Mesh. The fifth extends the way the Data Mesh entrusts quality to the domains, rather than to central certification of golden datasets. - Domain knowledge ownership: Principle 1, transposing domain-oriented ownership. Knowledge is embodied and partly tacit: the owner answers for it, not just stores it. - Knowledge as a self-describing product: Principle 2, transposing data as a product. There are two kinds of consumers, people and agents, and no base without a charter. - Self-serve knowledge platform: Principle 3, transposing the self-serve data platform. AI is not only hosted on the platform, it works inside it: it drafts, links and flags contradictions. - Federated knowledge governance: Principle 4, transposing federated computational governance. The goal is not to merge bases but to make them composable, through shared identifiers, metadata and open access protocols. - Auditable knowledge construction: Principle 5, extending quality assured by the domain. Knowledge quality is read through traceability: who proposed each change, who validated it, from which sources, and how to revert it. - The challenges of a Knowledge Mesh: The principles say what a Knowledge Mesh is; the challenges say what it must make possible. Fourteen questions fall into three families: managing knowledge, consuming it, and federating the bases. - Fundamentals before solutions: Solutions already address many challenges. The playbook starts one step earlier, with what must be true of knowledge for people and agents to rely on it; the answer shapes the choice of tools, and outlasts it. title: 6. The knowledge base
summary: The unit of the mesh, in seven parts: an entry point for legacy documents and a destination for generated ones, living alongside other bases.
text: Structure - An entry point - A destination - Bases that coexist Key ideas Key idea. The document is no longer the source of knowledge; it becomes one of its outputs. Concepts - Knowledge base: The unit and asset of the mesh: small enough to have one owner and one purpose, complete enough to be useful on its own. It has seven parts. - Compiled knowledge (LLM wiki): The pages of a base are the compiled layer Andrej Karpathy described as an "LLM wiki": knowledge assembled once and kept up to date, rather than reassembled at every question. - The document as output: Building a base turns legacy documents into an asset and audits what the organisation knows. Tomorrow, documents are produced from the base; what is generated never flows back without going through the management plane. - Bases that coexist: As bases multiply, the answer is coexistence rather than fusion. Each base keeps its owner, charter and pace; bases share identifiers, metadata and a common way to be reached. title: 7. The Knowledge Owner
summary: Authority, not probability: the person accountable for a base orients, arbitrates, commits, listens and retires, while agents take on the stewardship.
text: Structure - A commitment, dated and open to challenge Key ideas Key idea. The owner turns a probability into a commitment. title: 8. Dynamic context
summary: No delegation without grounding. Context assembled at the moment of use, from governed bases, within the rights of the person, and traceable.
text: Structure - The need for grounding - From prompt to dynamic context Key ideas Key idea. No delegation without grounding. Decisions and actions must be anchored in knowledge the company holds to be true, not in what a model finds plausible. Definition. Dynamic context is context assembled at the moment of use, from governed knowledge bases, within the rights of the person on whose behalf the agent acts. Concepts - Grounding: Grounding is the shared basis on which joint action rests. Decisions and actions must be anchored in knowledge the company holds to be true, not in what a model finds plausible. - Context engineering: Since 2025, practitioners have moved from prompt engineering to context engineering, the discipline of choosing what goes into a model's working memory. The Knowledge Mesh adds its organisational side. - Dynamic context: Context assembled at the moment of use, from governed knowledge bases, within the rights of the person on whose behalf the agent acts. It is the consumption plane at its most demanding. - Traceability: Every element of an agent's context points back to a page, and every page to its sources and its owner, so that whatever an agent relied on can be inspected afterwards. title: 9. Field guide
summary: Start small and real, treat the mesh as a trajectory, keep knowledge portable, and delegate to agents in three levels.
text: Structure - Start small, and real - The mesh is a trajectory - Interoperability - Three levels of delegation Key ideas Rule of thumb. Centralise the means, decentralise the knowledge. Concepts - Start small, and real: The first steps aim at a first base that is useful quickly, owned by someone and measured from the start: one domain, one owner, a one-page charter, the legacy compiled, an evaluation set. - The mesh is a trajectory: No company starts with a mesh: it starts with a common foundation, and the mesh appears as domains take ownership one after another. Centralise the means, decentralise the knowledge. - Interoperability and portability: A knowledge base is built to last longer than the technologies that serve it. The test: if the tool that built a base disappeared tomorrow, could the knowledge be read, moved and served by another one? - Three levels of delegation: Delegating to agents is a gradual decision, taken domain by domain, as trust grows. Assistance, delegation and autopilot are each reached on evidence. title: Why this playbook
summary: Four observations, about trust, organisation, pace and context, lead to an intuition: knowledge deserves to be managed as a pillar of AI, alongside data.
text: The foreword starts from early retrieval-augmented generation projects: answers still missed the mark, and the reflex was to fix them with the system prompt. The real question was elsewhere: what does the AI actually know about the company, in other words what context does it work from? One of the first avenues was to turn documents into question-and-answer pairs, to make visible what the AI sees; the gap with what people believed they had written was often a surprise, and a lesson. It shifted attention from documents to knowledge. Four observations follow: - Trust. As AI moves from answering to acting, delegating to an agent at scale requires understanding what it relies on: knowledge that can be read, owned and traced (see Authority, not probability, Three levels of delegation). - Organisation. An organisational gap cannot be fixed by prompt engineering alone. A better prompt does not give a document an owner, settle a contradiction or retire an outdated rule (see Knowledge Owner). - Pace. Technology moves faster than any plan; staying agile means investing in what lasts: how an organisation knows what it knows, and who stands behind it (see Interoperability and portability). - Context. Getting the best from AI is becoming a matter of giving agents the right context, and context is only as good as the data and knowledge it is drawn from (see Context engineering). From these observations comes the intuition that knowledge deserves to be managed as a pillar of AI, alongside data (Knowledge as a pillar of AI). The ambition is to help align a shared vision: a common foundation, the smallest set of principles that organisations, teams and technologies can share, so that each can translate it into its own context, at its own pace (see What stays open).
